title: API deployment
description: Resource requirements and operational wiring for the Stellar RWA API.
content: Deploying the Stellar RWA API The API is a long-running indexer. It keeps the latest decoded snapshot and query indexes in memory, while using Soroban RPC for polling. Size the service for the snapshot rather than treating it as a stateless request proxy.

title: API deployment › Resource profile
content: The following is a safe starting point for one network and a moderate workload: Resource Starting point Scale when CPU 1 vCPU polling, decoding, or concurrent requests saturate the process Memory 512 MiB the snapshot, decoded events, or query indexes approach the limit Disk 1 GiB ephemeral minimum logs or an optional local cache are retained Replicas 1 per indexed network each replica must have an independent poller/coordination policy Memory is workload-dependent. A large holder/event snapshot can require several times the baseline; set a container memory limit and alert before the process is OOM-killed. Do not run an unbounded number of pollers in the same process.

title: API deployment › Configuration
content: Set the RPC and deployment values in the service environment (names may vary by the API release): SOROBAN_RPC_URL=https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org RWA_NETWORK=testnet RWA_CONTRACT_ID=C... RWA_POLL_INTERVAL_MS=5000 RWA_METRICS_TOKEN=change-me PORT=8080 Keep credentials such as RWA_METRICS_TOKEN in the platform secret store, not in an image or a committed .env file. Use a separate deployment and contract ID for each network.

title: API deployment › Sample container deployment
content: services: rwa-api: image: ghcr.io/rwa-toolkit/stellar-rwa-api:latest restart: unless-stopped environment: SOROBAN_RPC_URL: https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org RWA_NETWORK: testnet RWA_CONTRACT_ID: ${RWA_CONTRACT_ID} RWA_METRICS_TOKEN: ${RWA_METRICS_TOKEN} PORT: "8080" ports: - "8080:8080" deploy: resources: limits: cpus: "1.0" memory: 512M

title: API deployment › Health and metrics
content: Configure the platform liveness probe to call GET /health . A successful response means the HTTP process is alive; it is not a guarantee that the poller is caught up. Scrape GET /metrics from a private network and send the bearer token configured by RWA_METRICS_TOKEN . Alert on stale poll timestamps, repeated RPC errors, process restarts, and memory pressure. Put a reverse proxy or network policy in front of both endpoints when they are exposed outside the cluster. During rollout, wait for /health and a recent poll timestamp in metrics before removing the previous instance. Keep graceful shutdown enabled so an in-flight poll can finish without publishing a partial snapshot.

title: API deployment › Self-host the documentation site
content: From the repository root, build the docs image with its public URL, then start the production Next.js server on port 3000. docker build --build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://docs.example.org -t stellar-rwa-docs ./docs docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 stellar-rwa-docs Pass other public settings from docs/.env.example with additional --build-arg flags. Rebuild the image when these values change.

title: FAQ
description: Short answers to recurring questions, each linking to the full explanation.
content: FAQ Short answers to the questions that come up most often. Each one links to the page that covers the topic in full.

title: FAQ › Do I need a wallet?
content: Not to read data. The API is read-only and needs no wallet, signing, or tokens — the Quickstart runs entirely against it. To issue, transfer, or claim through the web app you need the Freighter extension; the app signs through it and never holds keys. See Connecting Freighter .

title: FAQ › Is it on mainnet?
content: No. Everything is deployed on Testnet for demonstration and must not be used to custody real value. See the Network guide and the deployed contract addresses .

title: FAQ › How is compliance enforced?
content: In the contract itself. On every transfer (and on mint ), the asset-token contract calls the compliance contract to check the sender and recipient; if either fails, the transaction reverts. See How transfer gating works .

title: FAQ › Who counts as "allowed"?
content: An address passes is_allowed only if its KYC record is Approved , the approval has not expired, and its jurisdiction is not blocked. See How the allowlist model works and is_allowed .

title: FAQ › What happens when an approval expires?
description: What happens when an approval expires?
content: Once the current ledger reaches expires_at , is_allowed returns false : the holder can no longer transfer or receive the token until re-approved. There is no background job — expiry is checked live on every read. See KYC expiry and suspension .

title: FAQ › Why are times ledger numbers instead of dates?
description: Why are times ledger numbers instead of dates?
content: All on-chain and API time fields are Stellar ledger sequence numbers, and expires_at = 0 means "never". See Time & Ledgers , including converting ledgers to wall-clock time .

title: FAQ › Why was my transfer blocked?
content: Usually one of: pending approval, suspension, a blocked jurisdiction, an expired approval, not being on the allowlist, or the token being paused by the issuer. This is the compliance gate, not a bug — ask the issuer to approve your address. See What a failed gate looks like .

title: FAQ › Can an issuer block a whole country?
description: Can an issuer block a whole country?
content: Yes. block_jurisdiction makes every approved address in that jurisdiction fail is_allowed immediately; unblock_jurisdiction restores them. See Jurisdiction restrictions .

title: FAQ › How are dividends calculated?
content: Each holder claims total_amount * balance / total_supply , with balances read at claim time , not at a snapshot. See the Dividend contract and its security considerations .

title: FAQ › Does the API need authentication? Is it rate limited?
description: Does the API need authentication? Is it rate limited?
content: No authentication is required today. Rate limits and ETag caching are being introduced but are not yet enforced on Testnet. See Authentication and rate limiting and Rate Limits & Caching .

title: FAQ › How fresh is the API data?
description: How fresh is the API data?
content: The API polls Soroban RPC roughly every 10 seconds, so data lags the ledger by about that much, and it keeps serving the last snapshot if RPC is unreachable. For real-time state, read the contracts directly. See Data freshness and caching and Reading contracts directly .

title: FAQ › Why are amounts strings, and how do I display them?
description: Why are amounts strings, and how do I display them?
content: Token amounts are i128 on-chain, so the API serializes them as strings to avoid precision loss. They are raw base units — divide by 10 ** decimals . See the API Conventions .

title: Getting Started
description: What the Stellar RWA Toolkit is, how asset tokenization works, and how to run it.
content: Getting Started The Stellar RWA Toolkit is an end-to-end system for tokenizing real-world assets (RWAs) — real estate, invoices, commodities — on Stellar using Soroban smart contracts, with compliance enforced on-chain . It has three parts, each in its own repository: - Contracts — four Soroban contracts: asset-token , compliance , registry , dividend . - API — a Rust/Axum service that indexes all tokenized-asset activity and serves it over REST. - Web app — a Next.js front-end for issuers and investors.

title: Getting Started › What "tokenizing a real-world asset" means
content: A real-world asset — say a $5,000,000 Manhattan loft — is represented on-chain as a fungible token. Each token is a fractional claim on the underlying asset. Unlike an ordinary token, an RWA token is compliance-gated : only addresses that have passed KYC and sit on an allowlist may hold or receive it. The gate is not a policy sitting in a database — it is enforced by the contract itself. On every transfer, the asset-token contract makes a cross-contract call into the compliance contract to check both the sender and the recipient. If either fails, the transfer reverts. Securities laws in most jurisdictions restrict who may hold a regulated asset. Enforcing that restriction in the contract — rather than in an app that can be bypassed — is what makes a token suitable to represent a regulated real-world asset. See the Compliance Guide .

title: Getting Started › How the pieces fit together
content: ┌───────────────┐ issuer / investor ──▶ │ Web app │ ──▶ Freighter ──▶ Soroban contracts └───────────────┘ │ │ events + state ┌───────────────┐ polls Soroban RPC │ analysts / bots ──▶ │ REST API │ ◀─────────────────────┘ └───────────────┘ - The web app signs and submits transactions through the user's wallet. - The API only reads: it indexes on-chain state every 10 seconds and never holds a key or signs anything.

title: Glossary
description: Short definitions of the Stellar, Soroban and RWA terms used across these docs.
content: Glossary Terms are grouped by where they come from: Stellar, Soroban, and this toolkit's own domain vocabulary.

title: Glossary › Stellar
content: Ledger — One closed block of the Stellar network, roughly every 5 seconds. Each ledger has a sequence number that increases by one. Ledger sequence — The u32 counter identifying a ledger. The contracts use it as their only clock; see Time & Ledgers . Network passphrase — A string that identifies a Stellar network and is mixed into every transaction signature. A transaction signed for Testnet is invalid on any other network. Testnet — Stellar's public test network, where the toolkit is deployed. Its assets have no real value. Stroop — The smallest unit of XLM, one ten-millionth ( 0.0000001 ) of a lumen. Fees are quoted in stroops. Strkey — The base32 text encoding for Stellar keys and ids: account addresses start with G and contract ids start with C . Freighter — A browser wallet for Stellar that the web app uses to sign transactions. XDR — The binary format Stellar uses for transactions and ledger data. Clients usually see it base64-encoded.

title: Glossary › Soroban
content: Soroban — Stellar's smart-contract platform. Contracts are compiled to WebAssembly and run by the network's host. Soroban RPC — The JSON-RPC service used to simulate and submit contract calls and to read contract state and events. Host function — A function the Soroban runtime exposes to contracts, such as reading storage or calling another contract. ScVal — The XDR type for any value passed to or returned from a contract. Client libraries convert it with helpers like nativeToScVal and scValToNative . Simulation — A dry run of a contract call through simulateTransaction . It returns the result, the resource footprint and the fee without changing state, and is how read-only calls are made. Footprint — The list of ledger entries a transaction will read and write. It must be attached to a transaction before submission, which assembleTransaction does from a simulation. TTL (time to live) — How many ledgers a piece of contract storage stays live before it expires and is archived. Entries must be extended to be kept. Persistent storage — The contract storage type for data that must survive, such as KYC records. It is archived rather than deleted when its TTL runs out. Cross-contract call — One contract invoking another. The asset token calls the compliance contract this way on every transfer.

title: Glossary › Toolkit and domain
content: RWA (real-world asset) — An off-chain asset, such as property or an invoice, represented by an on-chain token. Asset token — The fungible token contract that represents ownership of one RWA. It is compliance-gated. See Asset Token . Registry — The contract that lists every tokenized asset and gives it a numeric asset id. Listing is self-attestation, not a compliance control. Allowlist — The set of addresses the compliance contract has a KYC record for. Only addresses that pass is_allowed may hold or receive the asset. KYC record — The compliance contract's per-address entry: status, jurisdiction, verified_at and expires_at . Approved / Pending / Rejected / Suspended — The four KYC statuses. Only Approved can pass is_allowed , and only while unexpired and outside a blocked jurisdiction. Jurisdiction — A two-letter ISO country code stored on a KYC record, such as US or KE . Issuers can block a whole jurisdiction at once. See the Compliance Guide . Transfer gate — The check the asset token runs on every transfer and mint: is_allowed must be true for the sender and the recipient. Expiry ( expires_at ) — The ledger at which a KYC approval lapses. 0 means it never lapses. See KYC expiry semantics . Valuation — The issuer-reported value of the underlying asset, stored in the registry in USD cents. It is not a market price. Distribution — A dividend payout announced through the dividend contract for holders of an asset token, which holders then claim. Claim — A holder's call to collect their share of a distribution. Balances are read at claim time. Indexer — The API's background poller that reads contract state from Soroban RPC about every 10 seconds and builds the snapshot the REST endpoints serve. Docs use "indexer" consistently (not "indexing service" or "indexing API") to match the indexer module name in the API source. Snapshot — The indexer's in-memory copy of contract state. Responses carry an ETag derived from its latest ledger.

title: Integration Guide
description: Query the API, use the TypeScript examples, and call the contracts directly.
content: Integration Guide Three ways to integrate with the platform, from easiest to most direct: 1. Query the REST API — indexed, JSON, no XDR. 2. Read contracts via the JS SDK — live simulation of view calls. 3. Submit transactions — sign with Freighter and invoke contract methods.

title: Integration Guide › API vs direct Soroban RPC access
description: API vs direct Soroban RPC access
content: Before you start, decide which read path fits your integration. The indexing API wraps Soroban RPC and returns decoded JSON; calling Soroban RPC directly gives you live on-chain state but requires more work on your side. Tradeoff Indexing API Direct Soroban RPC Latency Fast, single HTTP call returning pre-indexed JSON. One simulateTransaction round-trip per read; slower for multi-entity queries. Reliability Depends on the indexer staying in sync; may lag the chain by a few ledgers. Authoritative, always reflects current ledger state. Decode XDR No — responses are plain JSON with i128 as decimal strings. Yes — you build ScVal s and decode retval with scValToNative . Rate limits Governed by the API's own limits; cache-friendly and safe to poll. Subject to public RPC provider limits; heavy polling can be throttled. Best for Dashboards, listings, and UI reads that tolerate slight lag. Pre-transaction checks and reads that must be authoritative. Use the API for most reads and fall back to a direct RPC simulation only when you need the authoritative on-chain value — see Reading contracts directly .

title: Integration Guide › Querying the API
content: The REST API is the simplest integration surface. It is read-only and returns plain JSON. platform stats curl http://localhost:8080/stats all assets, then one asset's holders and dividends curl http://localhost:8080/assets curl http://localhost:8080/assets/1/holders curl http://localhost:8080/assets/1/dividends

title: Integration Guide › TypeScript client
content: const API = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:8080"; id: number; token_contract: string; name: string; symbol: string; asset_type: string; valuation_cents: string; valuation_usd: number; decimals: number; total_supply: string; holders: number; active: boolean; paused: boolean; compliance_contract: string; } const res = await fetch( ${API}/assets , { cache: "no-store" }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error( API ${res.status} ); return res.json(); } // Amounts are strings (i128) — parse with BigInt and format by decimals. const raw = BigInt(a.total_supply); const base = 10n ** BigInt(a.decimals); return (Number(raw) / Number(base)).toLocaleString(); } Always parse valuation_cents , total_supply , balance , and total_amount with BigInt(...) — they are decimal strings to preserve i128 precision.

title: Integration Guide › Reading contracts directly
content: To read live state without the API, simulate a view call with the Stellar JS SDK. No signing is required for reads. Contract, TransactionBuilder, Account, BASE_FEE, Networks, rpc, scValToNative, } from "@stellar/stellar-sdk"; const server = new rpc.Server("https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org"); const REGISTRY = "CBX5SMLTXX6JP4HA5GQIO2V6QM7WCUGL2GZ6D4U773HMRI6RXISKPUR3"; const contract = new Contract(REGISTRY); // Any valid account works as the simulation source. const source = new Account( "GAIQGTOBTTLLDJ4SWGGESM7UWJ2DI4K3ZNHUSHPDKJL2IE5FKY3BSRAA", "0", ); const tx = new TransactionBuilder(source, { fee: BASE_FEE, networkPassphrase: Networks.TESTNET, }) .addOperation(contract.call("total_value_locked")) .setTimeout(30) .build(); const sim = await server.simulateTransaction(tx); if (rpc.Api.isSimulationError(sim)) throw new Error(sim.error); return scValToNative(sim.result!.retval) as bigint; // USD cents } Check an address's compliance status the same way: const COMPLIANCE = "CBUERYDM7DXTZLLKDBRJKUBPFJ7M4OSUN4T7XKUARU345RLXNAIQD2IU"; const op = new Contract(COMPLIANCE).call( "is_allowed", new Address(investor).toScVal(), ); // build → simulate → scValToNative(retval) === boolean

title: Integration Guide › Submitting transactions
content: Writes must be signed by the account that authorizes them. In the browser, sign with Freighter: Contract, TransactionBuilder, Networks, BASE_FEE, rpc, Address, nativeToScVal, } from "@stellar/stellar-sdk"; const server = new rpc.Server("https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org"); token: string, from: string, to: string, amount: bigint, ): Promise { const account = await server.getAccount(from); const op = new Contract(token).call( "transfer", new Address(from).toScVal(), new Address(to).toScVal(), nativeToScVal(amount, { type: "i128" }), ); const built = new TransactionBuilder(account, { fee: BASE_FEE, networkPassphrase: Networks.TESTNET, }).addOperation(op).setTimeout(60).build(); // Simulate + assemble to attach the Soroban footprint and resource fees. const sim = await server.simulateTransaction(built); if (rpc.Api.isSimulationError(sim)) throw new Error(sim.error); const prepared = rpc.assembleTransaction(built, sim).build(); const { signedTxXdr } = await signTransaction(prepared.toXDR(), { networkPassphrase: Networks.TESTNET, address: from, }); const signed = TransactionBuilder.fromXDR(signedTxXdr, Networks.TESTNET); const sent = await server.sendTransaction(signed); return sent.hash; // then poll server.getTransaction(hash) } A transfer will revert with SenderNotCompliant (7) or RecipientNotCompliant (8) if either party is not KYC-approved. Check is_allowed for both addresses before submitting to give users a clear error up front.

title: Integration Guide › Worked example: check compliance before a transfer
description: Worked example: check compliance before a transfer
content: This walkthrough combines the compliance contract and the compliance API into one flow: given a sender and a recipient, verify both are is_allowed before attempting an on-chain transfer in the web app.

title: Integration Guide › 1. Read both statuses from the API
description: 1. Read both statuses from the API
content: The API exposes the same is_allowed check as the contract, so the UI can gate the transfer button without simulating a transaction: curl "http://localhost:8080/compliance/GSENDER.../is_allowed" curl "http://localhost:8080/compliance/GRECIPIENT.../is_allowed" const API = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:8080"; const res = await fetch( ${API}/compliance/${address}/is_allowed , { cache: "no-store", }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error( API ${res.status} ); const { allowed } = (await res.json()) as { allowed: boolean }; return allowed; }

title: Integration Guide › 2. Gate the transfer on both parties
description: 2. Gate the transfer on both parties
content: token: string, from: string, to: string, amount: bigint, ): Promise { const [senderOk, recipientOk] = await Promise.all([ isAllowed(from), isAllowed(to), ]); if (!senderOk) throw new Error("Sender is not KYC-approved"); if (!recipientOk) throw new Error("Recipient is not KYC-approved"); // Both allowed — safe to submit; the contract re-checks on-chain. return transfer(token, from, to, amount); }

title: Integration Guide › 3. Fall back to the contract for a live check
description: 3. Fall back to the contract for a live check
content: If you need the authoritative on-chain value (e.g. the API index is stale), simulate is_allowed directly against the compliance contract — the same call shown in Reading contracts directly : Contract, TransactionBuilder, Account, BASE_FEE, Networks, rpc, scValToNative, Address, } from "@stellar/stellar-sdk"; const server = new rpc.Server("https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org"); const COMPLIANCE = "CBUERYDM7DXTZLLKDBRJKUBPFJ7M4OSUN4T7XKUARU345RLXNAIQD2IU"; const source = new Account( "GAIQGTOBTTLLDJ4SWGGESM7UWJ2DI4K3ZNHUSHPDKJL2IE5FKY3BSRAA", "0", ); const tx = new TransactionBuilder(source, { fee: BASE_FEE, networkPassphrase: Networks.TESTNET, }) .addOperation( new Contract(COMPLIANCE).call( "is_allowed", new Address(address).toScVal(), ), ) .setTimeout(30) .build(); const sim = await server.simulateTransaction(tx); if (rpc.Api.isSimulationError(sim)) throw new Error(sim.error); return scValToNative(sim.result!.retval) as boolean; } The API check is a fast pre-flight; the on-chain simulation is the authoritative source of truth. Use both when correctness matters.

title: Indexer Metrics
description: Prometheus metrics exposed by the Stellar RWA API indexer.
content: Indexer Metrics GET /metrics (bearer token via RWA_METRICS_TOKEN ) exposes Prometheus text format. Names follow Prometheus conventions: rwa_indexer_ prefix, base units in the suffix ( _seconds ), and _total for counters. Metric Type Description rwa_indexer_refresh_duration_seconds histogram Poll (refresh cycle) duration. rwa_indexer_refresh_total{outcome} counter Refresh cycles, outcome is success or failure . Failures are the failure series. rwa_indexer_asset_read_errors_total{asset_id,read} counter Failed per-asset RPC reads. rwa_indexer_last_indexed_ledger gauge Ledger of the latest successful snapshot. rwa_indexer_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge Unix time of the last successful refresh. rwa_indexer_last_success_age_seconds gauge Lag: seconds since the last successful refresh, computed at scrape time. rwa_indexer_snapshot_assets gauge Assets in the in-memory snapshot. rwa_indexer_snapshot_events gauge Events in the in-memory snapshot. Suggested alert: rwa_indexer_last_success_age_seconds > 60 .

title: Performance & Benchmarks
description: What the indexer scaling benchmark measures and how to run it.
content: Performance & Benchmarks The Architecture page covers the API's steady-state performance characteristics (poll interval, rate limits, cache headers). This page covers how the indexer's scaling behavior — rebuild cost as the number of assets, holders, and distributions grows — is meant to be measured.

title: Performance & Benchmarks › What the benchmark measures
content: A Criterion benchmark at api/benches/registry_scaling.rs is the intended home for this: it would drive Indexer 's snapshot-rebuild path ( api/src/indexer/mod.rs ) against synthetic registries of increasing size — e.g. 10, 100, 1,000 assets, each with a realistic holder and distribution count — and report how refresh latency and allocation volume scale with dataset size. That is the number that matters for capacity planning: unlike HTTP response time (dominated by serialization, see Architecture ), the rebuild that runs once per POLL_INTERVAL is where cost actually grows with the size of the on-chain state being indexed. As of this checkout, api/benches/registry_scaling.rs and a [[bench]] target in api/Cargo.toml do not exist yet — rg "\[\[bench\]\]" api/Cargo.toml returns nothing. This page documents the benchmark's intended purpose and interface so that whoever adds it (and anyone reading Architecture 's reference to indexer scaling) has a concrete spec to implement against, rather than leaving the reference undocumented.

title: Performance & Benchmarks › Intended shape
content: api/Cargo.toml [dev-dependencies] criterion = "0.5" [[bench]] name = "registry_scaling" harness = false // api/benches/registry_scaling.rs (proposed) use criterion::{criterion_group, criterion_main, BenchmarkId, Criterion}; fn bench_rebuild(c: &mut Criterion) { let mut group = c.benchmark_group("snapshot_rebuild"); for &n_assets in &[10usize, 100, 1_000] { group.bench_with_input(BenchmarkId::from_parameter(n_assets), &n_assets, b, &n { let fixture = synthetic_registry(n); // N assets, holders, distributions b.iter( rebuild_snapshot(&fixture)); }); } group.finish(); } criterion_group!(benches, bench_rebuild); criterion_main!(benches);

title: Performance & Benchmarks › How to interpret results
content: - Report per-asset-count latency , not a single number — the question is how the curve bends as n_assets grows, since that's what determines how far the deployment scales before POLL_INTERVAL (10s) becomes too short to finish a rebuild comfortably. - Compare against POLL_INTERVAL . If rebuild time at the target asset count approaches a meaningful fraction of 10s, that's the signal to either raise POLL_INTERVAL , move state out of pure in-memory rebuild, or add a database (see the "no database in v1" note in API Overview ). - Run it locally (once added) with: `` bash cd api cargo bench --bench registry_scaling ` This only touches the api/` Rust workspace — it does not require the web app or docs site to be running.

title: Security Considerations
description: Trust assumptions, administrative authority, and the limits of on-chain compliance.
content: Security considerations for integrators This page describes what the Stellar RWA contracts and API can establish, what they cannot establish, and which actors must be trusted. It is implementation guidance, not legal, regulatory, custody, or security advice. The published deployment is Testnet-only and is not suitable for custody of real-world value. Do not treat a Testnet contract address, API response, or this documentation as evidence that an offering is legally compliant.

title: Security Considerations › Trust assumptions
content: - Contract code and deployment configuration: verify the exact contract IDs, WASM hashes, network passphrase, and SDK version in use. Contract IDs are network-specific. - Soroban RPC and the indexer API: RPC simulation and the REST API are useful read sources, but the API is a derived, polling snapshot rather than a source of settlement finality. For high-assurance decisions, independently query the chain and verify transaction results. - Keys and wallets: a signature proves control of an address, not the identity, authority, or intent of the person using it. Protect user sessions, key material, and transaction-review flows accordingly. - External token contracts: payment-token and compliance-contract calls are cross-contract dependencies. Their availability and behavior are part of the security boundary.

title: Security Considerations › Administrative authority
content: The contracts deliberately give administrators significant operational power: Contract Administrator can do Integrator implication Asset token Mint, pause/unpause, change valuation, replace the compliance contract Supply, transferability, valuation metadata, and the transfer gate can change. Compliance Approve, suspend, remove holders, and block jurisdictions An allowed holder can become unable to transfer immediately. Registry Register, deactivate, and curate asset records Registry visibility is not an independent verification of an asset or issuer. Dividend Create and fund distributions Claim amounts depend on the configured distribution and claim-time balances. Use multisignature controls, hardware-backed keys, documented incident response, and monitored governance for every administrator. Integrations should expose the admin-controlled nature of these actions rather than implying they are immutable protocol rules.

title: Security Considerations › Limits of on-chain compliance
content: The compliance contract enforces only its configured rules: an address must be approved, unexpired, and outside a blocked jurisdiction when the asset token calls is_allowed . It does not verify a person's real-world identity, beneficial ownership, accreditation, sanctions status, transfer restrictions in every jurisdiction, or whether off-chain records remain accurate. Jurisdiction strings, expiry ledgers, and allowlist records are inputs controlled by the compliance administrator. A successful transfer means the on-chain gate accepted those inputs at that ledger; it is not a regulatory determination or a guarantee of legal ownership.

title: Security Considerations › Integration practices
content: - Validate addresses, contract IDs, amounts, decimal precision, and network passphrases before building a transaction. - Simulate and review every transaction, then verify the submitted transaction reached a successful final ledger before treating a workflow as complete. - Treat indexer data as eventually consistent. Display its indexed ledger and handle stale or unavailable data rather than making irreversible decisions from it alone. - Keep an audit trail of the contract IDs, transaction hashes, timestamps, and off-chain approval evidence used for an action. - Design for pauses, compliance denials, RPC outages, and administrator key rotation. These are expected operational states, not impossible errors. See the individual asset-token , compliance , registry , and dividend references for method-level authority and error behavior.

title: Snapshot Memory
content: Snapshot Memory The indexer keeps a full snapshot (assets, holders, compliance, dividends, stats) in memory and rebuilds it every poll. Request handlers currently take a full Snapshot::clone() per request.

title: Snapshot Memory › Measurement
content: Each refresh records: - rwa_indexer_snapshot_estimated_bytes - approximate payload size (JSON length of every collection). Plot it against rwa_indexer_snapshot_assets to get bytes per asset; growth is linear in assets and in holders per asset. - rwa_indexer_snapshot_clone_duration_seconds - time of one full clone, which is the extra per-request cost of the current design.

title: Snapshot Memory › Strategy
content: 1. Serve requests from a shared Arc (the ArcSwap guard already provides one), so a request costs a pointer copy instead of a deep clone. 2. Cap per-asset holder lists in the snapshot and page the remainder on demand once rwa_indexer_snapshot_estimated_bytes approaches the container limit. 3. Alert on rwa_indexer_snapshot_estimated_bytes growth per asset before changing storage (a database is the step after paging).

title: Time & Ledgers
description: Understanding the ledger-sequence time model used across contracts and the API.
content: Time & Ledgers Throughout the Stellar RWA contracts and API, time is never expressed as a wall-clock timestamp. Instead, all time values use Stellar ledger sequence numbers — a monotonically increasing counter that increments roughly every 5 seconds on the Stellar network. This design eliminates time-sync issues and makes on-chain logic deterministic.

title: Time & Ledgers › Why ledger sequences?
content: - No clock skew. A ledger number is determined by network consensus, not server clocks. - Deterministic ordering. You can always compare ledger numbers to know which event happened first, without worrying about timestamp precision. - Simpler contracts. No need to worry about wall-clock adjustments or leap seconds.

title: Time & Ledgers › Ledger sequences in contracts
content: All on-chain time fields are u32 ledger sequence numbers: - Compliance contract: verified_at , expires_at (approval expiry) - Dividend contract: created_at (when a distribution was announced) - Registry contract: created_at (when an asset was registered) - Asset-token contract: clawback_at (when a clawback was performed)

title: Time & Ledgers › The special case: expires_at = 0 means "never"
content: When an expiry field (like expires_at in the compliance allowlist) is set to 0 , it means the permission never expires . This is a universal convention across all contracts: // Add a user to the allowlist with no expiry const op = compliance.call( "add_to_allowlist", admin, userAddress, "US", 0 // expires_at = 0 means never expires ); To set an expiry, provide a future ledger number: const server = new Horizon.Server("https://horizon.stellar.org"); const ledgers = await server.ledgers().limit(1).order("desc").call(); const now = ledgers.records[0].sequence; // Approve for 1 year (~6.3 million ledgers at ~5s per ledger) const expiresAt = now + 6_300_000; const op = compliance.call( "add_to_allowlist", admin, userAddress, "US", expiresAt );

title: Time & Ledgers › Checking expiry at runtime
content: The compliance contract's is_allowed gate checks expiry like this: // User is approved if: // (expires_at == 0) -- never expires, OR // (now = expires_at , the approval is considered expired and is_allowed returns false , blocking all transfers. No on-chain cron job is needed — expiry is enforced at read time.

title: Time & Ledgers › Ledger sequences in the API
content: The REST API mirrors this design. All time fields in responses are ledger sequence numbers , never wall-clock timestamps:

title: Time & Ledgers › Assets endpoint
content: { "id": 1, "name": "Manhattan Loft", "created_at_ledger": 3502885, "total_supply": "1000000" }

title: Time & Ledgers › Compliance endpoint
content: { "address": "GBUQWP...", "status": "Approved", "jurisdiction": "US", "verified_at": 3500000, "expires_at": 9800000, "expired": false } The expired field is a convenience boolean: true if expires_at != 0 && expires_at <= last_indexed_ledger .

title: Time & Ledgers › Dividends endpoint
content: { "id": 1, "asset_id": 1, "per_share_cents": "100", "created_at_ledger": 3510000, "payable_at_ledger": 3520000, "claimed": 500 }

title: Time & Ledgers › Converting ledger numbers to wall-clock time
description: Converting ledger numbers to wall-clock time
content: To convert a ledger number to an approximate wall-clock time, use the Horizon API: const server = new Horizon.Server("https://horizon.stellar.org"); const ledger = await server.ledgers().ledger(3502885).call(); console.log(ledger.closed_at); // "2026-05-15T10:30:00Z" Each ledger also records the wall-clock time it was closed, which you can use to estimate when a given ledger sequence number occurred. Rule of thumb: Stellar produces ~1 ledger per 5 seconds, so a ledger 1 million in the future is roughly 58 days away.

title: Time & Ledgers › Handling expires_at in your integration
content: When building an integration against the API: 1. Display the ledger number and the expired boolean. Don't try to calculate expiry yourself; trust the expired field from the API. 2. Refresh approval before expiry. If you're tracking approval expiry, call add_to_allowlist again before the expires_at ledger is reached. 3. Remember expires_at = 0 means never. Don't treat 0 as an epoch or default timestamp. 4. Use the API's expired field. The API already handles the comparison against the current indexed ledger for you.

title: Time & Ledgers › Common mistakes
content: - Treating ledger numbers as timestamps: They are not microseconds, milliseconds, or any other time unit. They are ledger sequence numbers only. - Forgetting that 0 means "never": Setting expires_at: 0 will create an approval that never expires, which may not be what you intended. - Assuming expiry is checked by a cron job: Expiry is enforced at read time ( is_allowed ). Once the current ledger passes expires_at , the approval is immediately and deterministically considered expired. - Comparing ledger numbers across different chains: Each Stellar network (testnet, public, futurenet) has its own ledger sequence counter. Do not assume a ledger sequence is portable between networks.

title: Time & Ledgers › What to read next
content: - Compliance Contract — expires_at and verified_at fields explained. - Compliance Guide — how expiry is enforced at read time by is_allowed . - API · Assets — created_at_ledger and indexed_at_ledger in the response. - Architecture Overview — how the indexer's polling interval affects ledger lag.

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common errors when integrating with the Stellar RWA API, and how to fix them.
content: Troubleshooting

title: Troubleshooting › CORS errors when calling the API from a browser
description: CORS errors when calling the API from a browser
content: You should not see these. The API sends a permissive CORS policy on every response — Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * , with all methods and headers allowed (see tower_http::cors::CorsLayer in api/src/routes/mod.rs ). There is no allowlist of origins to configure: any browser origin is permitted to call any endpoint. If a browser request is still being blocked, the request almost never reached the API's CORS layer in the first place. Check these, in order: This usually means the request failed before a response came back — a network error, a wrong URL, or a proxy/load balancer in front of the API that stripped the CORS headers. Open the Network tab and check the actual response status, not just the console error. - Request went to the wrong host or port. The API serves plain HTTP by default ( http://localhost:8080 locally). A typo'd base URL, or calling https:// against a server that only speaks http:// , fails before CORS is ever evaluated and surfaces as a CORS-shaped error in the console. - The request never left the browser. Mixed content (an https:// docs site calling an http:// API) is blocked by the browser itself, not by CORS, and also shows up as a CORS-style failure. - **A reverse proxy or CDN in front of the API dropped the Access-Control-* headers.** If you're running the API behind nginx, Cloudflare, or similar, confirm the proxy passes response headers through unmodified — some default configs strip unrecognized headers on error responses. - Preflight ( OPTIONS ) is being blocked upstream. Because allow_methods and allow_headers are set to Any , the API itself answers preflight requests for every method and header. If a proxy or firewall intercepts OPTIONS requests before they reach the API, the browser never gets a preflight response and the real request is blocked. - You're checking a 404 / 500 response for CORS headers. Error responses go through the same CorsLayer , so they carry the same headers as a success response. If a curl -i of the failing URL shows no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all, the response didn't come from this API — check for a proxy returning its own error page instead.

title: Troubleshooting › Quick check
content: curl -i -H "Origin: https://example.com" https://your-api-host/stats grep -i access-control A healthy response includes: access-control-allow-origin: * If that header is missing, the issue is upstream of the API (proxy, DNS, wrong URL) rather than CORS configuration — there is nothing to "allow" on the API side, since every origin is already allowed.

title: Versioning
description: How the Stellar RWA API and docs are versioned, and how breaking changes are communicated.
content: Versioning The API, the indexer and this documentation site are versioned together and follow Semantic Versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . - PATCH — bug fixes and docs corrections with no change to behavior or shape. - MINOR — backwards-compatible additions (new endpoints, new optional response fields, new query parameters). - MAJOR — breaking changes: anything that removes or renames a field, changes a field's type, changes default behavior, or removes an endpoint. Every breaking change is called out inline on the page it affects using the BreakingChangeCallout component, in addition to being listed in CHANGELOG.md at the repository root.

title: Versioning › Breaking change callout pattern
content: Use BreakingChangeCallout (in docs/components/BreakingChangeCallout.tsx , built on top of the shared CalloutBox ) to flag a breaking change directly on the reference page it affects: GET /assets/:id now returns tvl_cents as a string instead of a number to avoid precision loss in large totals. Update any client that parses it as a numeric type. This renders a red "Breaking change" box with the version it shipped in, so readers scanning a reference page cannot miss it. Keep the wording short: what changed, and what the consumer needs to do about it.

title: Versioning › Example
content: The API has not shipped a breaking change since the 0.1.0 initial release, so there is nothing to retrofit yet. The first time a response shape, field type, or endpoint is removed or changed incompatibly, add a BreakingChangeCallout to the affected reference page (for example docs/app/docs/api/overview/page.mdx or docs/app/docs/api/assets/page.mdx ) right above the section it changes, following the pattern above, and add a matching entry under a new ### Breaking changes heading in CHANGELOG.md .

title: Web App Guide
description: Connect Freighter, tokenize an asset, manage compliance, and distribute dividends.
content: Web App Guide The web app is the front-end for issuers and investors. It signs and submits every transaction through the user's Freighter wallet — it never holds keys. This guide walks through the main flows.

title: Web App Guide › Connecting Freighter
content: 1. Install the Freighter browser extension and create or import an account. 2. Switch Freighter to Testnet and fund the account via the friendbot . 3. In the app, click Connect Wallet and approve the connection. The app follows Freighter's selected network while connected, so reads and writes always target the same network. Your address appears in the header with a menu to copy it, view it on Stellar Expert, or disconnect. While disconnected you can still browse assets read-only and switch networks with the network selector. Once connected, the app locks to your wallet's network.

title: Web App Guide › Tokenizing an asset (issuer)
content: Open Tokenize an Asset and complete the multi-step form: 1. Asset info — name, type (real estate / invoice / commodity), description, and USD valuation. 2. Token config — symbol, total supply, and decimals. 3. Compliance — the initial set of KYC-approved addresses and their jurisdictions. Your own issuer address must be included , because the token mints the initial supply to you and that mint is compliance-gated. 4. Review & deploy — the app deploys the compliance contract and asset-token contract, then registers the asset in the registry. On success you get the deployed contract addresses with Stellar Expert links. Deployment is several transactions — a compliance contract, a token contract, and a registry registration. Approve each in Freighter as prompted. If you approve yourself last, the initial mint will fail; approve the issuer address in the compliance step first.

title: Web App Guide › Managing the compliance allowlist (issuer)
content: From the Issuer → Compliance page, select one of your assets: - Add an address — enter the account, choose a jurisdiction, and set an optional expiry. This calls add_to_allowlist and sets the status to Approved . - Suspend / remove — temporarily hold or permanently delete an approval. - Block a jurisdiction — freeze every holder in a country at once. The allowlist table shows each record's status, jurisdiction, and expiry. See the Compliance Guide for the model behind these actions.

title: Web App Guide › Creating dividend distributions (issuer)
content: From Issuer → Dividends , select an asset and open Create Distribution : 1. Choose the payment token (e.g. USDC on Stellar). 2. Enter the total amount to distribute. 3. Submit — the app calls create_distribution , which escrows the funds in the dividend contract. Holders then claim their proportional share. Each distribution shows a progress bar of claimed vs. total.

title: Web App Guide › Investor: compliance status and holdings
content: As an investor you can: - Check your compliance status on any asset's detail page and in your Portfolio . The app reads is_allowed and your KycRecord , and shows Approved / Pending / Suspended / Rejected / Not Registered . - Hold and transfer an asset — but only if you are approved. The transfer form is disabled with an explanatory message whenever you are not KYC-approved, the asset is paused, or your balance is zero. - Claim dividends — the app shows your claimable amount per distribution and a one-click Claim button that calls claim . If your transfer is blocked, the app tells you why — pending approval, suspension, a blocked jurisdiction, an expired approval, or simply not being on the allowlist. Ask the asset's issuer to approve your address. This is the compliance gate, not a bug.

title: Web App Guide › Transaction feedback
content: Every on-chain action shows live progress — preparing → awaiting signature → submitting → confirming — and, on success, a link to the transaction on Stellar Expert. Contract errors are translated into plain-language messages.

title: Build a Dashboard
description: Build a single-file TVL dashboard that reads /v1/stats and /v1/assets from the Stellar RWA API.
content: Build a Dashboard In this tutorial you build a one-file dashboard that shows the platform's total value locked (TVL), active asset count, holder count and a table of every asset. It reads two endpoints, /v1/stats and /v1/assets , and refreshes every 10 seconds, the same cadence the API's indexer uses. You need the API running locally, as described in Getting Started , and a browser. There is no build step and no framework.

title: Build a Dashboard › Step 1: Check the endpoints
content: With the API running on localhost:8080 , confirm both endpoints answer: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/stats curl http://localhost:8080/v1/assets /v1/stats returns one object. The dashboard uses tvl_usd , active_assets , total_assets , total_holders and last_indexed_ledger . /v1/assets returns an array. The dashboard uses name , symbol , asset_type , valuation_usd , holders , active and paused . Every data route is nested under /v1 . Requests to /stats or /assets without the prefix return 404 .

title: Build a Dashboard › Step 2: Create the dashboard
content: Create a file named dashboard.html and paste in this code: Stellar RWA Dashboard body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; margin: 2rem; color: #111; } .kpis { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; margin-bottom: 2rem; } .kpi { border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; padding: 1rem; } .kpi span { display: block; font-size: 0.85rem; color: #555; } .kpi strong { font-size: 1.5rem; } table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; } th, td { text-align: left; padding: 0.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid #eee; } .num { text-align: right; } #error { color: #b00020; min-height: 1.2rem; } #updated { color: #555; font-size: 0.85rem; } Stellar RWA Dashboard Total value locked — Active assets — Holders — Last indexed ledger — Asset Type Valuation Holders Status const API = "http://localhost:8080/v1"; const REFRESH_MS = 10_000; const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD", maximumFractionDigits: 0 }); const count = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US"); const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id); async function getJson(path) { const res = await fetch(API + path); const body = await res.json(); if (!res.ok) throw new Error( ${path}: ${body.error} (${body.message}) ); return body; } function renderStats(s) { $("tvl").textContent = usd.format(s.tvl_usd); $("active").textContent = ${s.active_assets} of ${s.total_assets} ; $("holders").textContent = count.format(s.total_holders); $("ledger").textContent = count.format(s.last_indexed_ledger); } function renderAssets(assets) { const rows = assets.map((a) => { const status = !a.active ? "Inactive" : a.paused ? "Paused" : "Active"; const tr = document.createElement("tr"); // textContent, never innerHTML: names and descriptions come from on-chain data. [ [ ${a.name} (${a.symbol}) , ""], [a.asset_type, ""], [usd.format(a.valuation_usd), "num"], [count.format(a.holders), "num"], [status, ""], ].forEach(([text, cls]) => { const td = document.createElement("td"); td.textContent = text; td.className = cls; tr.appendChild(td); }); return tr; }); $("assets").replaceChildren(...rows); } async function refresh() { try { const [stats, assets] = await Promise.all([getJson("/stats"), getJson("/assets")]); renderStats(stats); renderAssets(assets); $("error").textContent = ""; $("updated").textContent = Updated ${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()} ; } catch (err) { // Keep the last good numbers on screen and say that they may be stale. $("error").textContent = Could not load data: ${err.message} ; } } refresh(); setInterval(refresh, REFRESH_MS); The script runs two requests in parallel with Promise.all , so the page waits for the slower of the two rather than their sum.

title: Build a Dashboard › Step 3: Serve it from an allowed origin
description: Step 3: Serve it from an allowed origin
content: Do not open dashboard.html with a file:// URL. The browser sends a null origin, and the API will not allow it. Serve the folder over HTTP instead: cd path/to/dashboard python3 -m http.server 5500 The API allows browser requests only from http://localhost:3000 by default. That is the docs site's dev server, so it will not work for a page on port 5500 . Add your origin in api/.env , then restart cargo run : api/.env RWA_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:3000,http://localhost:5500 Open http://localhost:5500/dashboard.html. The four tiles fill in on the first refresh, and the table lists every asset the API knows about. If the tiles stay at — and the browser console shows a CORS error, the origin serving the page is missing from RWA_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS . Fix that before debugging the code.

title: Build a Dashboard › How it works
content: - Amounts are numbers here, on purpose. tvl_usd and valuation_usd are floats, which is fine for display. For exact arithmetic, use the string fields tvl_cents and valuation_cents , and parse them with BigInt . See Assets . - Untrusted text uses textContent . Asset names and descriptions come from on-chain data that anyone can register. Inserting them with innerHTML would let a crafted name run script in your page. - Failures keep the old numbers. If a refresh fails, the error appears above the tiles and the last good values stay on screen. A 404 or 400 returns a JSON body with error and message . See Errors . - Polling is steady, not bursty. Each refresh makes two requests, one every 10 seconds per open tab. If many visitors will keep the page open, raise REFRESH_MS and check the Rate Limits & Caching page.
